The Keeper's Ledgers
The ferry to Carrow Island ran twice a day in summer and,
after the first week of October, only when the harbormaster
felt like it. Nora Pell took the 7:40 crossing on a Tuesday,
with one suitcase, a borrowed raincoat and a letter from a
solicitor she had never met.
The letter was short. Her great-uncle, Edmund Pell, had
died in March at the age of 91. He had left her the keeper's
cottage at Carrow Light, its contents, and "such papers as
may be found therein." There was no money to speak of.
There was, the solicitor added, a small matter of unpaid har-
bor dues amounting to £38.
She had met Edmund exactly once, at a wedding in 1987,
when she was nine. He had given her a brass button and told
her it came from the coat of a drowned captain. Her mother
said afterwards that he had bought a bag of them in a market
in Hull.
The crossing took fifty minutes. A man in a yellow jacket
checked her ticket twice, the second time apparently for
something to do. "You'll be the niece," he said. "Great-niece,"
said Nora. He nodded as though this confirmed a rumor.
"He kept the books, you know. Right up to the end."
"What books?"
"The light's books. Every ship, every night." He looked
out at the water. "Nobody asked him to. The light's been au-
tomatic since 1994."
